summary.text: A 16-year-old girl presented with vomiting, blood in urine and jaundice over four days. Laboratory results showed severe anemia, a low platelet count, deranged kidney function with urea 118 mg/dL and creatinine 3.61 mg/dL, elevated bilirubin and schistocytes above 5% on the smear. Direct Coombs, infection screens, ANA and vasculitis profile were negative, C3 was reduced and C4 normal.

Anti-factor H antibodies were negative. Targeted exome sequencing found a homozygous CFHR1/CFHR3 deletion classified as a variant of uncertain significance; it was not confirmed with MLPA or microarray, with financial constraints given as a reason. Renal biopsy was not done. The patient was managed for atypical HUS with plasma exchange and pulse methylprednisolone.

Her condition improved with treatment, with hematological remission and renal function recovery within three and seven days respectively; Table 2 lists hematological recovery at 3 days and full recovery in 7 days.

summary.text: A 12-year-old girl had body swelling, paleness, hematuria and reduced urine output for about a week, with episodes of vomiting. She was conscious with elevated blood pressure, pallor, icterus and edema, without organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, kidney dysfunction, 10% schistocytes and elevated LDH.

Renal biopsy confirmed features of thrombotic microangiopathy, with glomerular basement membrane duplication, mesangiolysis, endothelial swelling and a tram-track appearance on silver stain. She had a high anti-factor H antibody level. Financial constraints limited her genetic testing and treatment options.

She received plasma infusion therapy with methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide. Hematological response was observed in five days, but renal function did not improve, with progression to chronic kidney disease requiring maintenance dialysis.

summary.text: A four-year-old boy with a history of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome treated with tacrolimus, who had received two doses of rituximab one month earlier, presented with fever, multiple facial pustules, facial swelling and paleness. His condition worsened with sepsis and acute kidney injury.

Laboratory tests showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, deranged kidney function, schistocytes 6%, reticulocytes 10.5%, negative ANA, low C3 and normal C4; a renal biopsy confirmed thrombotic microangiopathy. He had low IgG for age and received intravenous immunoglobulin, and anti-factor H antibodies were negative. Whole-exome sequencing found a homozygous CFH missense variant, likely pathogenic.

He received plasmapheresis followed by plasma infusions and dialysis. Hematological remission was achieved in 12 days, but acute kidney injury persisted and he continued on maintenance hemodialysis before the parents took him home against medical advice because of financial constraints.

On arrival she showed respiratory failure from pulmonary edema and cardiac failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Renal biopsy was not done.

Because of the high anti-factor H autoantibody she was started on plasmapheresis and methylprednisolone pulse therapy. She showed gradual improvement with hematological remission, but her acute kidney injury showed limited recovery.

Upon admission she was in respiratory failure due to pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock and required intubation, mechanical ventilation and immediate hemodialysis.

Laboratory investigations showed hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes and renal impairment, and a renal biopsy indicated HUS with focal tubular necrosis. Following treatment with hemodialysis, plasma infusion, steroids and mycophenolate mofetil, she achieved hematological remission in three days and showed significant improvement in kidney function within 10 days; Table 2 lists PLEX rather than plasma infusion.

summary.text: A 10-year-old girl presented with generalized body swelling and paleness for 15 days and severe generalized headaches with blurring of vision, dizziness and vomiting, with no history of jaundice, loose stool, seizure or altered sensorium.

Laboratory tests showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia with platelet count 55 x 10^9/L, kidney dysfunction with creatinine 2.18 mg/dL, 10% schistocytes and elevated LDH, and a high anti-factor H antibody level. Renal biopsy was not done, and financial constraints limited her genetic testing and treatment options.

She received plasma infusion therapy with steroids and mycophenolate mofetil. Hematological response was observed in five days but renal function showed partial improvement only, and her parents took her home against medical advice because of financial constraints.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status is not_inspected; actual images were inspected in the separate visual submission.
Table 1 columns Case 1 to Case 7 are matched to Patients 1 to 7 by case order and by identical values in each patient narrative; the table itself does not label them as the same people.
Cohort statements (for example three patients with anti-FH antibodies in the Results versus five in the Discussion and Table 1, median age, percentages) are not copied to individuals.
Figure 3 and Figure 4 captions describe zygosity opposite to the Patient 5 and Patient 6 narratives and Table 2; recorded as review-only source conflicts and not resolved from pixels.
The Discussion sentence about a previous child whose father died at 42 years of age does not name the patient and is not assigned.
Table 2 hematological recovery (days) cells are recorded as the cell value under that header without a literal duration phrase where the narrative gives none.
The Patient 7 urea is printed 84.38 mg/dL in the narrative and 84.3 in Table 1; both are kept as linked representations of one measurement (rounding-level ambiguity).

The Table 2 treatment cell for Patient 5 lists PLEX where the narrative says plasma infusion; the plasma therapy type is a review-only source conflict. Table 2 alone lists hemodialysis for Patient 6 (kept, with an ambiguity about possible misalignment).

The Results paragraph says anti-FH antibodies were detected in three (43%) patients, while Table 1 shows five positive values and the Discussion refers to five patients with anti-FH-associated HUS; this cohort-level inconsistency does not change the per-patient Table 1 and narrative results.
Table 2 says renal biopsy was suggestive of TMA for Patients 2 and 3 while the narratives say it confirmed TMA; recorded as ambiguities.
